item.title: Farmer guilty of rape
item.description: A FARMER has been convicted by the High Court in Labasa for raping his cousin’s partner after following her into a house under the pretext of making a phone call. Justice Lee James Burney found the 35-year-old guilty of one count of rape earlier this month.
item.content:encoded:
A FARMER has been convicted by the High Court in Labasa for raping his cousin’s partner after following her into a house under the pretext of making a phone call.

Justice Lee James Burney found the 35-year-old guilty of one count of rape earlier this month.

The incident occurred on the morning of October 6, 2023, when the 20-year-old victim returned indoors wearing only a towel after doing laundry and bathing.

The court was told the man entered the residence to make a phone call due to cellular coverage in the area, before grabbing the victim by the waist, pulling her onto a mattress, and raping her.

The victim fought back, managed to escape across a river to a relative’s house, and reported the assault.

The man denied the allegations, claiming he was framed over an ongoing farming dispute between him and his cousin.

Justice Burney found the victim to be a truthful and unshaken witness whose prompt report to relatives supported her credibility.

The man was given 30 days to appeal to the Court of Appeal.

item.title: Vosanibola opts to continue with trial
item.description: FORMER parliamentarian Peceli Vosanibola has opted to continue his corruption-related trial rather than have the matter start afresh. His lawyer Mesake Waqavanua confirmed the defence’s position to Magistrate Joseph Daurewa during a hearing under Section 139 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2009 last week.
item.content:encoded:
FORMER parliamentarian Peceli Vosanibola has opted to continue his corruption-related trial rather than have the matter start afresh.

His lawyer Mesake Waqavanua confirmed the defence’s position to Magistrate Joseph Daurewa during a hearing under Section 139 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2009 last week.

This followed the court’s earlier ruling that Mr Vosanibola had a case to answer to two charges brought by the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC).

Mr Waqavanua told the court the defence wanted the trial to continue before Magistrate Pulekeria Low, who had heard the prosecution’s case and witnesses.

FICAC prosecutor Setefano Komaibaba agreed, saying a fresh trial could prejudice the prosecution if witnesses were unavailable or unable to return to court.

Mr Vosanibola is charged with providing false information to a public servant and obtaining a financial advantage.

FICAC alleges he falsely declared in 2019 that his permanent residence was Navuloa Village, Ovalau, while allegedly residing in Nadera, Nasinu.

It is further alleged that he obtained a financial advantage of $19,749.50 through allowance claims between August 2019 and March 2020. A ruling on the Section 139 application will be delivered on September 16.

item.title: DPM: Expect reforms in business landscape
item.description: DEPUTY Prime Minister and Trade Minister Manoa Kamikamica says Fiji’s efforts to attract investment should not depend on one person, as he looks ahead to the next election and works to make it easier to do business in Fiji. Mr Kamikamica said the Government’s focus should instead be on strengthening systems and processes that would continue to support investors regardless of who holds political of
item.content:encoded:
DEPUTY Prime Minister and Trade Minister Manoa Kamikamica says Fiji’s efforts to attract investment should not depend on one person, as he looks ahead to the next election and works to make it easier to do business in Fiji.

Mr Kamikamica said the Government’s focus should instead be on strengthening systems and processes that would continue to support investors regardless of who holds political office.

His comments came after he was asked whether he hoped to attract more investors if he stood in the next election, following positive feedback from investors about his accessibility and understanding of their concerns.

“The restructuring is currently underway and is focused heavily on digital transformation, which would significantly improve Fiji’s investment environment,” Mr Kamikamica said.

He pointed to investor permits and company registration as areas where faster processing could make a difference.

“If, for example, investor permit takes seven days. Company registration takes, in New Zealand, it now takes 24 hours. If that can happen in Fiji, in this genuine digital transformation, that will put Fiji on a different platform and make it more attractive to invest.”

Mr Kamikamica said one of the main considerations for investors was how easy it was to establish and operate a business in a country.

He acknowledged that while Fiji was relatively easy to do business in, challenges remained.

However, he said work was already underway to address some of those obstacles, including efforts between Fiji and Australia to integrate systems that could improve the approval of permits.

“If that is successful, when successful, should mean some significant changes in how permits are approved.

“So yeah, the doors are always open for conversations and obviously trying to find more opportunities for Fiji.”

Mr Kamikamica said Fiji already had an advantage as an attractive and welcoming destination, but improving the business environment could further strengthen its appeal to investors.

item.title: Defence seeks acquittal
item.description: DEFENCE has urged the High Court to acquit Nigel Yogesh Singh of arson, arguing the State failed to prove he intentionally or recklessly set fire to the historic Queen Victoria School clubhouse in Toorak, Suva. In closing submissions last week, Legal Aid lawyer Etonia Veibataki argued that prosecution evidence and forensic findings raised competing explanations for the fire.
item.content:encoded:
DEFENCE has urged the High Court to acquit Nigel Yogesh Singh of arson, arguing the State failed to prove he intentionally or recklessly set fire to the historic Queen Victoria School clubhouse in Toorak, Suva.

In closing submissions last week, Legal Aid lawyer Etonia Veibataki argued that prosecution evidence and forensic findings raised competing explanations for the fire.

Mr Veibataki submitted the blaze may have been accidentally started by a lit mosquito coil and argued there was no evidence establishing the required criminal intent.

He also pointed to evidence from prosecution witnesses who, under cross-examination, said they saw no candles or deliberate use of accelerants at the scene. State lawyer Pio Navara, however, argued two witnesses testified that Mr Singh had been warned repeatedly about the consequences of lighting a candle inside the clubhouse.

Mr Navara submitted Mr Singh voluntarily and recklessly lit the candle despite knowing the risk of fire and had no lawful excuse for being in the clubhouse.

Justice Dane Tuiqereqere will deliver his judgment on September 22.

item.title: Court: Interim injunction stays
item.description: THE High Court in Lautoka has upheld an interim injunction restraining popular social media personality Ana Masere from verbally abusing and posting alleged defamatory comments about Nadi businessman King Anwar Hussain on social media. Justice Anare Tuilevuka delivered the ruling on August 20, maintaining the ex-parte injunction originally granted against Ms Masere in April 2025.
item.content:encoded:
THE High Court in Lautoka has upheld an interim injunction restraining popular social media personality Ana Masere from verbally abusing and posting alleged defamatory comments about Nadi businessman King Anwar Hussain on social media.

Justice Anare Tuilevuka delivered the ruling on August 20, maintaining the ex-parte injunction originally granted against Ms Masere in April 2025.

The court order restrains Ms Masere from making abusive posts regarding Mr Hussain, also known as “Buddha”, on social media platforms pending the final determination of the substantive lawsuit.

Mr Hussain initiated legal action after Ms Masere published a video post alleging he engaged in indecently assaulting girls and making derisive remarks about his anatomical features.

In her defence, Ms Masere claimed the comments were not directed at any identifiable person and argued the court order infringed on her constitutional right to freedom of expression.

Rejecting her arguments, Justice Tuilevuka held that freedom of expression is not absolute and does not shield false statements that undermine an individual’s right to dignity, privacy, and reputation.

The court noted that given the long-standing business association between both parties and the fact that Mr Hussain is publicly known by the name used in the post, a reasonable reader within their social circuit could identify him as the subject.

The court ruled that serious allegations of indecent assault, if false and directed at an identifiable individual, amount to defamation.

Ms Masere was also ordered to pay $1000 in costs to Mr Hussain within 21 days.

item.title: New status promises major changes
item.description: Navua’s historic entry into Fiji’s municipal map came at a cost of around $100,000 with Government saying the bigger task now is turning the new status into real development for the town. Speaking in an interview after the formalities, Local Government Minister Maciu Nalumisa said the funding was already allocated in the current financial year for the transition and development of the new municipa
item.content:encoded:
Navua’s historic entry into Fiji’s municipal map came at a cost of around $100,000 with Government saying the bigger task now is turning the new status into real development for the town.

Speaking in an interview after the formalities, Local Government Minister Maciu Nalumisa said the funding was already allocated in the current financial year for the transition and development of the new municipality.

He said the budget allocation was made to accommodate the facility and the more than 4000 people expected to attend the historic occasion.

He said the next move would be the installation of a new administration to oversee the town’s transition.

Mr Nalumisa said the Government was now finalising the names of special administrators who would manage the new Navua Town Council during the transition period.

He said the appointments were expected to be made in the coming months, subject to approval by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka.

“They’ll all be appointments, and we’re going to appoint people from Navua,” he said.

He said beyond administration, the transition was expected to bring major physical changes.

Mr Nalumisa said the Department of Town and Country Planning was working towards a revised town planning scheme as the existing central business district was too small.

This included the new bus stand, carrier stand and market area, while the existing recreational park could also be relocated.

He said the Government had already made a budget allocation for the work.

He said the funds spent on the declaration was justified by the significance of the occasion.

Mr Nalumisa said the declaration marked a new chapter for Navua, with improved infrastructure and development expected as the town moves through its transition to municipal governance.

“This is a historical day for Navua, and for the people of Navua.”

item.title: BACK IN HISTORY | Letter unites family
item.description: LETTERS have been known to cause tragedy, create wonderful opportunities and even change the course of history. For Abraham Cadigan, however, one letter brought about what he described as a “happy reunion” of family members who never thought they would meet.
item.content:encoded:
LETTERS have been known to cause tragedy, create wonderful opportunities and even change the course of history.

For Abraham Cadigan, however, one letter brought about what he described as a “happy reunion” of family members who never thought they would meet.

The Fiji Times reported on October 17, 1990, that Mr Cadigan, then about 60, had been reunited with relatives in Papua New Guinea after generations of separation.

Mr Cadigan traced the family’s roots to his ancestor, Ned Cadigan, an Irishman who “came to Fiji in the early 19th century and married a Fijian woman”.

“Two of them went and settled in Papua New Guinea and raised families there,” Mr Cadigan said.

“The other two remained here and also raised families.”

Over the years, members of the Cadigan family in Fiji had tried to establish contact with their relatives in Papua New Guinea.

It took a letter from Lucy English, a member of the Papua New Guinea branch of the family, to finally bridge the gap.

Mrs English described writing the letter as “making a stab in the dark”.

She said she had written from Papua New Guinea in “a desperate attempt” to locate her maternal great-great-great-grandfather’s family.

“I addressed it simply to ‘Cadigan’ and sent it through a friend who was visiting Fiji,” she said.

The letter eventually reached Abraham, who replied with what Mrs English described as a “sentimental but sincere letter”.

“I couldn’t believe it! It was a very happy moment for me when I received the letter.

“After four generations, I had finally established contact with my great-grand-uncle’s family members.”

The discovery was equally emotional for Mr Cadigan’s family.

“The letter brought tears to my eyes,” Mrs English said.

“It was wonderful to know that our family was in Fiji.

“And to locate, after all those attempts to locate our family, we are reunited.”

Mr Cadigan explained that the separation had begun when two of the brothers migrated to Papua New Guinea.

“Since the two brothers migrated, there was no contact,” he said.

“In our young days we were always told stories of how our granduncles were separated.

“I always wanted to contact my relatives in PNG, but all my attempts proved fruitless.”

Four members of the Papua New Guinea-based Cadigan family had arrived in Suva the previous month to attend the wedding of one of their relatives, Jackie Cadigan, who was marrying Tui Kabu, son of Pastor Aisake Kabu, then president of the Seventh-day Adventist Church’s Central Pacific Union Mission.

The wedding was scheduled for 4pm that day at the Seventh-day Adventist Church in Tamavua.

Members of the Cadigan family in Fiji had initially known nothing about the wedding.

“But one thing led to another, and here we are,” Mr Cadigan said, as he pointed to members of the clan preparing at his Delainavesi home for the “big and happy event”.

Mrs English summed up the extraordinary reunion simply.

“Everything has turned out so beautifully.

“The wedding is the icing on the reunion cake.”

Members of the Cadigan clan from Savusavu also joined the family gathering in Suva. For Mr Cadigan, it was more than a wedding. It was the long-awaited coming together of a family separated for generations.

item.title: POINT OF ORIGIN | A life built on faith and perseverance
item.description: KEOLA Pati’s life has been shaped by work, family, faith and perseverance. From her early working days, when she travelled by speedboat to island resorts to sewing curtains, to raising a family through difficult times and working for decades in Fiji’s furniture and retail industries, she learned to keep going regardless of the circumstances. She faced fear, financial hardship, loss and uncertainty
item.content:encoded:
KEOLA Pati’s life has been shaped by work, family, faith and perseverance. From her early working days, when she travelled by speedboat to island resorts to sewing curtains, to raising a family through difficult times and working for decades in Fiji’s furniture and retail industries, she learned to keep going regardless of the circumstances.

She faced fear, financial hardship, loss and uncertainty, but also experienced the kindness of workmates and people who helped her along the way.

Now, 86, and still working, Keola’s story offers a glimpse into a generation shaped by discipline, responsibility and the belief that when there is work to be done, you simply do it.

For a young Keola Pati, the water rushing past was frightening. She watched the boat cut across the sea, carrying her towards an unfamiliar island and a job she had agreed to take.

She was going to work on an island in the Mamanuca Group.

That moment, many decades ago, would become one of countless moments in Keola’s life when fear could have stopped her — but did not.

Today, she can look back on a life defined not by the absence of hardship, but by her determination to keep going through it.

For Keola, the foundation of her life was laid in childhood.

Her parents were her first teachers, teaching her the responsibilities and expectations that shaped the woman she would become.

“The first teacher used to be our parents.”

At home, there was little room for questioning.

“They teach us, you do this, you do that, you do that.”

You woke up, did what needed to be done and carried on.

When Keola began working, those childhood lessons became reality.

“When I start to work, I wake up in the morning, I go to work, do the job then come back home, then do the cooking, washing, everything.”

There was always something to do but hardship also taught her endurance.

When she first started working at Hensher (Fiji) Ltd, – a UK-based household manufacturing company that operated in Fiji during the 1970s and 1980s – her boss asked if she could go to the Reef Hotel for work.

The materials and machines were loaded onto a boat and Keola went with them.

Her job was to measure and sew curtains.

It was the beginning of a working life that would take her to different islands, including Mana Island and Castaway Island.

For a young woman travelling alone for work, it was an experience filled with unfamiliar surroundings and moments of fear.

The first speedboat journey remains vivid in her memory.

Working away from home brought other challenges.

One night, while staying on an island, Keola saw a snake near her door.

“I was so frightened. I can’t yell, I can’t do anything. I just pray to God, ‘please God, you help me’.”

For Keola, the experience reinforced something she had learned from her parents — faith. Prayer became a constant part of her life.

It travelled with her wherever work took her.

“Only prayer can change things. Nothing else.

“Anything you want to do, first you pray to God. You must pray when the sun rise.”

Her faith became a source of strength during the difficult years that followed.
